title: Bilal, the Voice That Would Not Break
period: Dawn of Islam, Mecca and Medina
teaser: A slave with no clan and no wealth lay under a rock on the burning sand of Mecca. He would become the first voice to call Muslims to prayer.
story:
A man lies on the burning sand outside Mecca, a heavy rock on his chest. His master, Umayya ibn Khalaf, wants only one thing: that he give up his new faith. Tradition relates that Bilal answered with a single word, repeated again and again: Ahad, Ahad — One, One.

Bilal ibn Rabah was a slave of Abyssinian origin, and one of the very first people in Mecca to accept Islam. He had no clan to protect him, no wealth, no rank. All he had was his conviction, and it proved stronger than the stone. Abu Bakr, a close companion of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, finally bought him and set him free.

Years later, in Medina, the Muslims needed a way to call people to prayer. The Prophet ﷺ chose Bilal, whose voice carried far. The freed slave became the first muezzin of Islam. The early biographies relate that when the Muslims entered Mecca, Bilal gave the call to prayer from the top of the Kaaba, in the very city where he had been tortured.

He died in Syria around the year 640. Fourteen centuries later, the call he was the first to raise still rises five times a day all over the world.
lesson: A person's worth does not come from origin, wealth or status, but from what they stand for. Hold on to what you know is true, even when you seem to stand alone.

title: Al-Khwarizmi and the Book That Named Algebra
teaser: He wanted to help people divide inheritances and measure fields. His book gave the world the word algebra, and his name gave it the word algorithm.
story:
Baghdad, around the year 820. A scholar is writing a book for a very practical reason: people need help dividing inheritances, measuring land, digging canals and settling trade accounts. He is Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, and his name points to Khwarazm, a region of Central Asia south of the Aral Sea.

He works in the time of the caliph al-Ma'mun, a great patron of learning. In his book he explains, step by step, how to solve problems in which a quantity is unknown. One of the operations he uses is called al-jabr, which means restoring or completing. The word stands in the title of his book, and from it comes our word algebra.

Surprisingly, the book contains no symbols at all: no x, no equals sign. Everything is written in full sentences, with clear examples and geometric figures to show why each method works.

In the twelfth century the book was translated into Latin, and European scholars learned from it for generations. Another of his works explained the Indian way of writing numbers with nine digits and a zero. In Latin his name became Algoritmi, which gave us the word algorithm. Each time a phone or a computer runs a program, it echoes the name of a scholar from Baghdad.
lesson: The most lasting knowledge often begins with a wish to be useful. Explain things clearly, step by step, and your work can serve people you will never meet.

title: Fatima al-Fihri and the Mosque of al-Qarawiyyin
teaser: She inherited a fortune and, tradition says, gave all of it away. What she founded in Fez in 859 is still open today.
story:
Fez, in the middle of the ninth century. A woman has just inherited a fortune from her father, a merchant. She could spend it on a comfortable life. Instead, tradition relates, she decides to give all of it to build a mosque for her community.

Her name is Fatima al-Fihri. According to the Moroccan chroniclers, her family had come to Fez from Kairouan, in present-day Tunisia, along with many other migrants. The mosque she founded, in the year 859, took the name of their quarter: al-Qarawiyyin, the mosque of the people of Kairouan. The same accounts say that she fasted until the building was finished, and that her sister Maryam founded another mosque across the river, the mosque of the Andalusians.

What we know of Fatima comes from accounts written several centuries later, and historians treat the details with caution. But the building is very real. Enlarged by one dynasty after another, al-Qarawiyyin became one of the great centres of learning of the Muslim world, where students came to study law, grammar, mathematics and astronomy.

It is still open today. It is often described as the oldest university in the world still in operation, born from one woman's decision to turn an inheritance into a gift.
lesson: What you keep for yourself ends with you; what you give to learning can outlive you by a thousand years. Ask what your means, large or small, could build for others.

title: Ibn Battuta: He Left for Mecca and Kept Going
period: Marinid Morocco and the wider Muslim world
teaser: At twenty-one he left Tangier alone to make the pilgrimage. He came home for good almost thirty years later, having seen most of the known world.
story:
In June 1325, a young man of twenty-one rides out of Tangier, in Morocco. He writes later that he left alone, with no companion and no caravan, sad to leave his parents. His plan is simple: to perform the pilgrimage to Mecca. He will not come home for good for nearly thirty years.

His name is Ibn Battuta. After the pilgrimage, curiosity carries him further and further: Iraq and Persia, the coast of East Africa, Anatolia, the steppes of Central Asia, then India, where the sultan of Delhi makes him a judge. He serves as a judge again in the Maldives, and his account takes him as far as China, though historians debate some stages of the route. Late in life he crosses the Sahara to visit the empire of Mali.

Trained in Islamic law, he finds almost everywhere a mosque, fellow scholars and a welcome. In all, he is thought to have covered about 120,000 kilometres, probably more than any other traveller known before modern times.

Back in Morocco, the sultan asks him to dictate his memories to a writer named Ibn Juzayy. The book, known as the Rihla, the Journey, was finished around 1355. It remains one of our best windows onto the fourteenth-century world.
lesson: A first step taken with a sincere purpose can lead much further than you imagined. Stay curious about people who live differently from you, and write down what you learn.

title: Cordoba: A Forest of Columns
teaser: The columns were too short for a great hall, so the builders stacked one arch on top of another. Their solution became one of the most famous sights in the world.
story:
Step inside, and you seem to enter a forest of stone: hundreds of columns, row after row, carrying double arches striped in red and white. This is the Great Mosque of Cordoba, in southern Spain.

It was begun around 785 by Abd al-Rahman I, an Umayyad prince who had fled Syria as a young man, crossed North Africa and founded a new state in al-Andalus. His builders reused columns from older Roman and Visigothic buildings. Because these were short, they placed a second arch above the first to raise the ceiling: a practical solution that became the building's signature.

Over two centuries, as Cordoba grew into one of the largest cities in Europe, his successors enlarged the mosque again and again. In the tenth century the caliph al-Hakam II added a magnificent mihrab, the niche showing the direction of prayer, decorated with gold mosaics made with the help of craftsmen sent from Byzantium.

In 1236 Cordoba was taken by the king of Castile, and the mosque became a cathedral; in the sixteenth century a church nave was built in its centre. Yet the forest of arches still stands, and people come from all over the world to walk through it.
lesson: A limit can become a signature: the builders' short columns produced their most beautiful idea. When your means fall short, look for the clever solution instead of giving up.

title: Ibn Sina and the Canon of Medicine
period: Samanid Central Asia and Buyid Persia
teaser: As a teenager he cured a ruler and asked for one reward: access to the royal library. His medical encyclopedia was taught for centuries, from Persia to Europe.
story:
At sixteen he was already treating patients. At about eighteen he was called to the bedside of the ruler of Bukhara, and what he gained from it was the thing he wanted most: permission to use the royal library.

This is how Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, tells his own youth in his autobiography. Born around 980 near Bukhara, in present-day Uzbekistan, he says he had memorised the Qur'an by the age of ten. His adult life was far from calm: as dynasties rose and fell, he moved from court to court across Persia, serving as physician and sometimes as minister, writing wherever he stopped.

His great medical work is the Canon of Medicine. In five books, it organises the medical knowledge of his time: the principles of medicine, simple remedies, diseases of each part of the body, illnesses that affect the whole body such as fevers, and compound medicines. Its strength was its order: a doctor could find what he needed.

Translated into Latin in the twelfth century, the Canon was taught in European universities for centuries, in some places until the seventeenth century. Ibn Sina died in 1037 in Hamadan, in Iran, where his tomb is still visited.
lesson: Knowledge becomes useful to others when it is put in order. Read widely while you are young, then take the trouble to organise what you know so that others can use it.

title: Mansa Musa, the Pilgrim King of Mali
teaser: In 1324 a West African king crossed the Sahara on his way to Mecca. He gave away so much gold in Cairo that its price was still low twelve years later.
story:
Cairo, 1324. A caravan arrives from across the Sahara, so rich that the city will talk about it for years. At its head rides Musa, the mansa — the king — of Mali, on his way to Mecca for the pilgrimage.

His empire, in West Africa, drew great wealth from the gold trade. Musa and his companions gave away and spent so much gold in Cairo that the metal lost value there. The scholar al-Umari, who visited the city about twelve years later, wrote that its price had still not recovered. The exact size of the caravan is unknown; the figures given by later writers are impossible to verify.

But Musa brought back more than fame. He returned with scholars and books, and with an Andalusian poet and architect, Abu Ishaq al-Sahili. Tradition credits al-Sahili with the great Djinguereber mosque of Timbuktu, a city that would become a famous centre of learning.

News of the journey travelled far. In 1375, a map drawn in Majorca, the Catalan Atlas, showed the king of Mali seated on a throne, holding a nugget of gold. Far to the north, people who had never crossed the Sahara now knew of his kingdom, through the journey of a pilgrim king.
lesson: Wealth is remembered for what it built, not for how brightly it shone. Whatever you gain, invest part of it in knowledge and in things that will serve others.

title: Baghdad and the House of Wisdom
teaser: In Baghdad, scholars of several faiths worked side by side to translate the knowledge of the ancient world into Arabic, and then to go beyond it.
story:
In ninth-century Baghdad, a Christian physician, a Muslim mathematician and a Sabian astronomer from Harran could find themselves bent over the same books. What brought them together was one of the great efforts of human history: translating the knowledge of the ancient world into Arabic.

The Abbasid caliphs, especially al-Ma'mun, who ruled from 813 to 833, supported this movement. At their court stood the Bayt al-Hikma, the House of Wisdom. Historians debate exactly what it was — probably a royal library where scholars and copyists worked — and the translation movement was much wider, paid for by many patrons. But the name has come to stand for the whole adventure.

Works of Greek medicine, mathematics, astronomy and philosophy, along with Persian and Indian texts, were sought out, sometimes far away, and translated with care. Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a Christian from Iraq, translated a large part of the works of the physician Galen, comparing several manuscripts to establish a reliable text.

Scholars did not only translate: they checked, corrected and went further. Al-Khwarizmi wrote his algebra in this Baghdad. Centuries later, much of this knowledge reached Europe through Latin translations made from Arabic.
lesson: Knowledge grows when people are humble enough to learn from those who came before, whatever their origin. Take the best of what others have found, check it, and add your own part.

title: How Paper Changed the World of Books
teaser: A simple sheet made from old rags travelled from Samarkand to Baghdad, then to Spain. Wherever it arrived, books multiplied.
story:
A sheet of paper seems like nothing. Yet when it reached the Muslim world, in the eighth century, it changed how knowledge was kept and shared.

Paper had been invented in China many centuries earlier. A famous account, written down long afterwards, says that Chinese prisoners taken at the battle of Talas, in Central Asia, in 751, taught the craft in Samarkand. Historians doubt that it happened so simply: paper was probably already known in the region. What is certain is that Samarkand became famous for its paper, made from linen and hemp rags.

From there the craft travelled west. By about 800, paper was being made in Baghdad, and the Abbasid administration adopted it for its records. Paper was cheaper than parchment, which was made from animal skins, and easier to obtain than Egyptian papyrus. The effect was enormous. Books multiplied; Baghdad had a whole market of booksellers and copyists; great libraries appeared. Scholars could own more books, and students could take notes.

Papermaking then spread to Syria, Egypt, North Africa and al-Andalus, where the town of Xàtiva was known for its paper by the twelfth century. From Spain and Italy it later spread across the rest of Europe.
lesson: A humble tool can change more lives than a famous monument. Never look down on what is simple and cheap if it helps knowledge reach more people.

title: How the Qur'an Was Gathered Into One Book
teaser: After a battle in which many who knew the Qur'an by heart were killed, a worried Companion went to see the caliph. A young scribe was given a task he found heavier than moving a mountain.
story:
The year is about 633. At the battle of Yamama, many of those who knew the Qur'an by heart have just been killed. Umar ibn al-Khattab is worried and goes to the caliph Abu Bakr: if more memorisers die, part of the revelation could be lost. He urges him to gather the whole Qur'an in writing.

Abu Bakr hesitates at first: how could he do something the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ had not done? Then he is convinced. He entrusts the task to a young man, Zayd ibn Thabit, who had been one of the Prophet's scribes. Zayd later said that moving a mountain would have seemed lighter to him. He collected the text from pieces of parchment, palm stalks, flat stones and the memories of men. The finished sheets were kept by Abu Bakr, then by Umar, then by Umar's daughter Hafsa.

Some years later, under the caliph Uthman, Muslims lived from Egypt to Persia. A Companion named Hudhayfa returned from a campaign alarmed: people were disputing over how to recite. Uthman had a group led by Zayd make copies from Hafsa's sheets, and sent them to the great cities.

The Qur'an that Muslims read all over the world today follows the written text of those copies.
lesson: What is precious must be protected before it is in danger, not after. Listen to the person who warns you early, and do carefully the work that others will rely on.

title: Ibn al-Bawwab, the Doorkeeper's Son
period: Abbasid Caliphate under the Buyids, Baghdad
teaser: The son of a doorkeeper became the most admired calligrapher of Baghdad. One Qur'an written by his hand has survived for more than a thousand years.
story:
His name means the doorkeeper's son, and that is exactly what he was: the child of a man who guarded a door in Baghdad. He began, it is said, as a house decorator. He became the most admired calligrapher of his age.

Ibn al-Bawwab lived in Baghdad around the year 1000 and died there around 1022. A century before him, the vizier Ibn Muqla is credited with rules giving each Arabic letter fixed proportions, measured in dots made by the pen. Ibn al-Bawwab took up this proportioned writing and gave the rounded scripts a new elegance and regularity. Such scripts had mostly been used for letters and ordinary books; in his time they came to be used for copies of the Qur'an as well.

He is said to have copied the Qur'an sixty-four times. Only one of those copies is known today: a small volume written on paper in Baghdad in the year 391 of the Hijra, 1000–1001, now kept in the Chester Beatty Library in Dublin. Its lines are so even that they look effortless.

Generations of calligraphers, from Iraq to Turkey, learned by imitating his style. Clear, well-proportioned Arabic writing owes much to the doorkeeper's son.
lesson: Excellence is not inherited; it is built with patient practice. Whatever your craft, the care you put into small strokes is what makes the whole page beautiful.

title: Ibn al-Haytham and the Dark Room
teaser: For centuries, great minds believed that our eyes send out rays to see. In Cairo, one man decided to stop arguing and start testing.
story:
For centuries, many of the greatest minds believed that we see because our eyes send out rays that touch the objects around us. In Cairo, about a thousand years ago, a man set out to test that idea, and overturned it.

Al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham was born in Basra, in Iraq, around 965. Medieval biographers relate that he was invited to Egypt to regulate the floods of the Nile, realised the project was impossible, and pretended to be mad to escape the anger of the ruler. Whatever the truth of that story, it was in Cairo that he wrote his masterpiece, the Book of Optics, in seven volumes.

His method was new. He did not simply reason: he experimented. In a darkened room, he let light enter through a small hole and studied how it travelled in straight lines. He showed that vision happens when light, coming from objects, enters the eye, and not the other way round. He insisted that claims be checked by testing.

Translated into Latin, his book was studied in Europe for centuries, and scholars such as Roger Bacon and Kepler built on it. The word camera itself recalls a dark room: camera obscura, in Latin.
lesson: Do not accept an idea just because it is old or because famous people held it. Test it, and be ready to change your mind when the evidence asks you to.

title: Aisha, the Teacher of Medina
teaser: When the Companions were unsure about something the Prophet ﷺ had said or done, they often went to ask the same person. For more than forty years, her home was a school.
story:
In Medina, when the Companions of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ were unsure about what he had said or done, they often knew where to go. They went to ask Aisha.

Aisha bint Abi Bakr, wife of the Prophet ﷺ and daughter of his closest friend, had lived at his side and observed his daily life: how he prayed, how he fasted, how he behaved at home. She had a sharp mind and an excellent memory, and she asked questions when she did not understand.

After the Prophet's death in 632, she lived for more than four decades, and her home became a place of learning. Men and women came to question her. More than two thousand hadith are transmitted on her authority, which places her among the few Companions who narrated the most. She did not only repeat: she explained, and she corrected others when she judged that they had misunderstood or misremembered.

Among her students were her nephews Urwa ibn al-Zubayr and al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, and a woman scholar, Amra bint Abd al-Rahman; all three became leading teachers of the next generation. Urwa is reported to have said that he had seen no one more learned than her in law, medicine and poetry. She died in Medina around 678.
lesson: Pay attention, ask questions, and remember: what you learn carefully today, you may be the one to teach tomorrow. Sharing knowledge accurately is one of the greatest services to others.

title: Zheng He, the Admiral From Yunnan
teaser: Born into a Muslim family in south-west China and captured as a boy, he rose to command some of the largest fleets the world had yet seen.
story:
In 1405, a fleet leaves the mouth of the Yangtze: dozens of enormous ships and many smaller ones, carrying about 27,000 men. Its admiral is a Muslim from the far south-west of China.

He was born around 1371 in Yunnan, with the name Ma He. His father and grandfather both bore the title hajji, which suggests that they had made the pilgrimage to Mecca. As a boy he was captured by the armies of the Ming dynasty, made a court servant, and placed in the household of a prince. He grew into a trusted officer; when the prince became the Yongle emperor, he gave him a new name, Zheng He, and later command of the imperial fleet.

Between 1405 and 1433, Zheng He led seven great voyages across the Indian Ocean: to Java and Sumatra, to India, to Hormuz in the Persian Gulf, to Arabia and down the coast of East Africa. The fleets carried silk and porcelain, and brought back envoys, spices and even a giraffe. During the last voyage, some of his companions travelled to Mecca.

He died around 1433. His voyages had linked China to the Muslim ports of the Indian Ocean decades before European ships reached those waters.
lesson: A hard beginning does not decide where a life will end. Do faithfully the work in front of you, and you may be trusted with far greater things.

title: Al-Zahrawi, the Surgeon of Cordoba
teaser: After nearly fifty years of practice, a surgeon from al-Andalus drew and explained about two hundred instruments, so that his students would not have to guess.
story:
Open the last part of his encyclopedia and you find something no earlier surviving medical book offers in such number: drawings of surgical instruments, about two hundred of them. Scalpels, forceps, hooks, probes, each one explained.

Their author, Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi, lived near Cordoba in the tenth century, when al-Andalus was at its height. His name comes from Madinat al-Zahra, the palace city built by the caliphs outside Cordoba. Europe would later call him Albucasis.

After nearly fifty years of practice, he gathered everything he knew into a work in thirty parts, the Kitab al-Tasrif, completed around the year 1000. He wrote it, he explains, for his students, whom he calls his children. The final part deals with surgery: how to cauterise, to set broken bones, to treat wounds, to help in difficult births. He describes stitching inside the body with thread made from animal gut. He also warns his readers: a surgeon must know anatomy thoroughly, must weigh the danger before operating and must never act out of greed.

Translated into Latin in the twelfth century, his treatise on surgery was copied, quoted and later printed in Europe, where surgeons relied on it for centuries. Some of the instruments he drew are recognisable in operating theatres today.
lesson: Real masters do not guard their secrets; they explain them so that others can do better. Write down what experience has taught you, and pass it on generously.

title: The Alhambra, the Red Palace of Granada
teaser: A small kingdom surrounded by stronger neighbours built one of the most delicate palaces on earth, and wrote the same humble sentence all over its walls.
story:
On a hill above Granada, the same short Arabic sentence is carved on wall after wall, again and again: There is no victor but God. It was the motto of the Nasrids, the last Muslim dynasty of Spain, and it says a lot about the palace they built.

The Nasrid kingdom was founded in the thirteenth century, at the very time when most of al-Andalus was being lost. It was small and surrounded by stronger neighbours. Yet it lasted about two and a half centuries, and on that hill its rulers built the Alhambra — from al-Hamra, the red one, after the colour of its walls.

From outside it is a plain fortress. Inside, mostly in the fourteenth century, craftsmen created some of the most delicate rooms ever built: carved plaster as fine as lace, coloured tiles in geometric patterns, ceilings like honeycombs, and verses of poetry running along the walls. Water, brought from the river by a canal, flows through courtyards and fountains, the most famous of them carried by twelve stone lions.

In January 1492, Granada surrendered to the Catholic Monarchs of Spain. The palace survived, and it is today among the most visited monuments in Spain.
lesson: Beauty does not need size or power; it needs care and humility. Even in an uncertain time, you can make something fine that will outlast your worries.

title: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: Power as a Trust
teaser: Raised as a prince, he became ruler of an empire stretching from Spain to Central Asia, and chose to live simply. He ruled for little more than two years and was never forgotten.
story:
In 717, a man learns that he has just been named ruler of an empire stretching from Spain to Central Asia. Tradition relates that he received the news as a burden, not a prize.

Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz was a prince of the Umayyad family, raised in comfort, and through his mother a great-grandson of the caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab. Once caliph in Damascus, the accounts agree, he changed his way of life. He gave up luxury and handed over to the public treasury wealth that he judged his family had no right to keep; tradition adds that his wife Fatima gave up her jewels too.

He listened to complaints against governors and removed those who were unjust. He lightened unfair taxes. He also wrote to scholars asking them to gather the sayings of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in writing, for fear that knowledge would disappear with those who carried it — an important step in the history of hadith collection. Later writers relate that in some provinces, the officials in charge of charity struggled to find anyone poor enough to receive it.

He died in 720, not yet forty, after little more than two years in power. Muslims have remembered him ever since as a model of the just ruler.
lesson: Authority is a responsibility to carry, not a privilege to enjoy. Wherever you are in charge, at home, at school or at work, begin by being strict with yourself.

title: Al-Jazari and His Ingenious Machines
teaser: A court engineer described about fifty machines in such detail that they can still be rebuilt today. Among them: a water clock in the shape of an elephant.
story:
An elephant carries a tower on its back. At regular intervals the figures on it come to life: a bird whistles, a serpent tips forward, the elephant's driver moves. It is a clock, driven by water, and it was designed more than eight hundred years ago.

Its inventor, al-Jazari, was an engineer at the court of the Artuqid princes in Diyar Bakr, in what is now south-eastern Turkey, where he served for about twenty-five years. In 1206, at his ruler's request, he completed a book describing about fifty machines: clocks, fountains, vessels that pour drinks by themselves, devices for washing hands and machines for raising water.

Two things make the book exceptional. First, the mechanisms: one of his pumps uses a crank and connecting rod to turn rotation into back-and-forth movement, a principle found today in car engines. Second, his method. He explains that he describes only what he has built and tested himself, and he gives measurements and drawings so that other craftsmen can build the machines in turn.

Several of his devices have been rebuilt in modern times by following his descriptions, and they work. The proof of a good explanation is that someone else, centuries later, can make the thing again.
lesson: An idea is only finished when it has been built and tested. Do not just imagine: make it, check that it works, and explain it clearly enough for others to repeat.

title: How Islam Sailed to the Malay World
teaser: Islam first reached the islands of Southeast Asia not with armies but with merchants, carried by the monsoon winds from port to port.
story:
Islam did not first reach the islands of Southeast Asia with an army. It came by ship, with merchants, on the monsoon winds.

For centuries, traders from Arabia, Persia and India had sailed to the ports of Sumatra, Malaya and Java in search of spices, on the sea route to China. Many were Muslims. They settled in the harbour towns, married there and built mosques; scholars and Sufi teachers followed. Little by little, local rulers adopted the faith of their trading partners.

In northern Sumatra, the gravestone of Sultan Malik al-Salih, ruler of the port of Samudra-Pasai, bears the date 1297: it is one of the oldest traces of a Muslim kingdom in the region. When Ibn Battuta stopped there half a century later, he found a sultan who loved discussing religious law with scholars.

In the fifteenth century the rulers of Malacca, a new port on the strait between Malaya and Sumatra, became Muslim as well. Malacca grew into one of the busiest harbours in the world, and its language, Malay, written in Arabic letters, helped carry the faith from island to island. Today, Indonesia and Malaysia together are home to well over two hundred million Muslims.
lesson: People are convinced by how you behave long before they listen to what you say. Honest dealing in everyday life is the most powerful message you can carry.

title: The Bimaristan: A Hospital Open to All
teaser: In 1284 a hospital opened in Cairo whose charter welcomed everyone, rich or poor, free of charge. The secret of its funding was a gift designed never to run out.
story:
Cairo, 1284. A new hospital opens its doors, and its founding charter sets out who may be treated there: everyone. Rich and poor, men and women, free people and slaves, residents and strangers, without payment.

It was built by Sultan Qalawun and known as the Mansuri hospital. Men and women had separate wards. There were sections for different conditions — fevers, eye diseases, wounds, stomach illnesses — as well as a pharmacy, kitchens and a place for teaching medicine. The physician Ibn al-Nafis left it his library.

Such a hospital was called a bimaristan, from a Persian word meaning place of the sick. The first were founded in Baghdad from about the year 800, and others followed in Damascus, in Cairo, and from Anatolia to al-Andalus. Doctors made their rounds with their students.

How was all this paid for, with free care? Through the waqf: a founder gave property — shops, land, baths — whose income was reserved for the hospital for ever. It could not be sold or inherited. The gift went on working long after the giver had died. The Mansuri hospital cared for patients for centuries, and parts of its building still stand in Cairo.
lesson: The best generosity is organised to last. When you want to do good, think about how it can keep working after the first enthusiasm, and even after you.

title: Mus'ab ibn Umayr, the First Envoy
period: Dawn of Islam, Mecca and Medina
teaser: He was the best-dressed young man in Mecca. He gave it all up, and was sent alone to teach a city that would change history.
story:
In Mecca, everyone knew Mus'ab ibn Umayr: the young man from a wealthy family, with the finest clothes and perfume. Then he accepted Islam. The early biographies relate that his mother, furious, shut him in and cut him off from the family's wealth. He chose his faith, and a much poorer life.

Around the year 621, a small group from Yathrib — the oasis that would soon be called Medina — pledged themselves to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ sent Mus'ab back with them to teach them the Qur'an. He was the first envoy of Islam.

In Yathrib he stayed with As'ad ibn Zurara and taught patiently. Two clan leaders, Usayd ibn Hudayr and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, came one after the other intending to stop him; he invited each to sit and listen first. Both accepted Islam, and many of their people followed. A year later, more than seventy men and women from Yathrib came to pledge their support to the Prophet ﷺ. The city was ready to welcome him.

Mus'ab was killed at the battle of Uhud in 625, carrying the Muslims' banner. His companions related that the only cloth they had for his shroud was too short to cover him completely.
lesson: Gentleness opens doors that force cannot. When someone comes to you angry, invite them to sit and listen first; patience and good manners are often the strongest argument.

title: Al-Biruni Measures the Earth From a Mountain
period: Ghaznavid Empire, Central Asia and India
teaser: With one mountain, one instrument and some geometry, a scholar from Central Asia worked out the size of the whole Earth, and came remarkably close.
story:
On a height near the fort of Nandana, in what is now Pakistan, a scholar aims his instrument at the horizon. He has no ship, no team of surveyors, no need to cross a desert. With one mountain and some geometry, he intends to measure the whole Earth.

Abu Rayhan al-Biruni was born in 973 in Khwarazm, in Central Asia. In the early eleventh century he came to India in the wake of the armies of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni. While others looked for treasure, he looked for knowledge: he studied Sanskrit, talked with Indian scholars and wrote a large, fair-minded book describing India's sciences, beliefs and customs.

His idea at Nandana was elegant. First he measured the height of the mountain. Then, from its top, he measured how far the horizon dipped below a level line. From that small angle and the mountain's height, trigonometry gave him the radius of the Earth. His result was remarkably close to the value we know today.

Earlier scholars had measured the Earth by having teams pace out long distances across flat plains. Al-Biruni showed that one careful observer could do it alone. He left behind well over a hundred works, most of them now lost.
lesson: A good method is worth more than great resources. Before saying a task is too big for you, look for the clever angle from which it becomes possible.

title: Sinan, the Architect Who Kept Learning
teaser: He became chief architect at about fifty and worked for another half-century. He called one of the great mosques of Istanbul the work of an apprentice.
story:
He was about fifty when he was named chief architect of the Ottoman Empire, an age at which many careers are winding down. His would last another half-century.

Sinan was born around 1490 in a Christian village of central Anatolia. As a young man he was recruited into the sultan's service, became a Muslim and joined the Janissaries. On campaign from the Balkans to Iraq, he learned his craft the hard way, building bridges, fortifications and ships as a military engineer.

In 1539 Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent put him in charge of imperial building. Sinan served three sultans, and the lists of his works drawn up in his own time count more than three hundred: mosques, schools, hospitals, baths, bridges, aqueducts.

He never stopped trying to do better. According to the memoirs he dictated to a friend, he considered the Şehzade Mosque in Istanbul the work of his apprenticeship, the Süleymaniye that of his maturity, and the Selimiye in Edirne, finished when he was in his eighties, his masterpiece. Its great dome rests on eight pillars above a hall flooded with light. He died in 1588 and rests in a modest tomb he designed himself, beside the Süleymaniye.
lesson: It is never too late to begin, and never time to stop improving. Treat each thing you finish as a lesson for the next one.

title: Timbuktu, the City That Treasured Books
period: Mali and Songhai empires, West Africa
teaser: In a market on the edge of the Sahara, a visitor noticed that handwritten books sold for more profit than any other goods. Families have guarded those books ever since.
story:
In sixteenth-century Timbuktu, on the southern edge of the Sahara, a visitor noted something that surprised him: among all the goods sold in the market, handwritten books brought in more profit than any other merchandise.

That visitor is known as Leo Africanus, and the city he described was at its height. Enriched by the trade in gold and salt, Timbuktu had become, under the Mali and then the Songhai empires, a city of scholars. Around its mosques, especially Sankore, teachers gave lessons in law, grammar, astronomy and medicine. Books were imported across the desert, copied by hand and commented on by local authors, in Arabic and sometimes in African languages written in Arabic script. The most famous of these scholars, Ahmad Baba, who died in 1627, said that his library of about 1,600 volumes was smaller than those of others in his family.

The books survived because families kept them, generation after generation, in chests. In 2012, when armed conflict reached the city, librarians and ordinary residents secretly carried a very large part of the manuscripts to safety, trunk by trunk.

Timbuktu had grown rich on gold and salt. What its people chose to save, when danger came, was their books.
lesson: A community shows what it truly values by what it protects in hard times. Take care of books and of the knowledge handed down to you; they are an inheritance for those who come after.

title: Al-Idrisi Maps the World for a King
teaser: In Palermo, a Muslim geographer spent about fifteen years questioning travellers for a Christian king. The result was one of the most detailed descriptions of the world of its time.
story:
Palermo, Sicily, in the 1140s. At the court of a Christian king, a Muslim scholar is gathering reports from travellers: where they have been, how many days separate one town from the next, what grows there and what is sold. The accounts are compared, and what the witnesses agree on is kept; what they contradict is set aside.

The king is Roger II, a Norman ruler whose island is home to Latin and Greek Christians, Muslims and Jews. The scholar is al-Idrisi, born around 1100 in Ceuta, on the coast of North Africa. Roger has asked him for nothing less than a description of the whole known world.

The work took about fifteen years. It was completed in 1154, shortly before the king died. It is a great book of geography, often called the Book of Roger, which divides the world into seventy sections, each with its own map, from the Atlantic to China. The maps place south at the top, as was common among Muslim mapmakers. Al-Idrisi also had a large map of the world engraved on silver, which has since been lost.

For a long time his work remained one of the most detailed descriptions of the world ever made. It was born of a simple method: ask, compare, verify.
lesson: Before repeating something, check it against more than one source. Reliable knowledge is built by asking, comparing and keeping only what holds up.

title: Ibn al-Nafis and the Path of the Blood
period: Ayyubid and Mamluk Syria and Egypt
teaser: In 1924 a student opened an old manuscript in Berlin and found a discovery about the heart, written in Cairo three centuries before Europe described it.
story:
In 1924, a young Egyptian doctor studying in Germany examined an old Arabic manuscript kept in Berlin, and found in it a discovery that the history books credited to Europeans of three centuries later.

The author was Ibn al-Nafis. Born near Damascus around 1213, he studied medicine at the city's Nuri hospital and then settled in Cairo, where he became chief physician of Egypt. Around 1242 he wrote a commentary on the anatomy in Ibn Sina's Canon.

For more than a thousand years, doctors had followed the Greek physician Galen, who taught that blood passed from the right side of the heart to the left through invisible pores in the wall between them. Ibn al-Nafis said plainly that there are no such pores: the wall is solid. Blood from the right side, he wrote, must travel to the lungs, mix there with air, and return to the left side of the heart. He had described the circulation of blood through the lungs.

His insight seems to have been little noticed in his own time. He kept working and writing until his death in Cairo in 1288, and left his house and his books to the new Mansuri hospital.
lesson: Respecting your teachers does not mean repeating their mistakes. Say what the evidence shows, calmly and honestly, even if recognition comes late or never.

title: The Astrolabe-Maker of Aleppo
teaser: Almost everything known about her fits in one line of an old book. Yet that single line tells of a woman who built precision instruments for a prince.
story:
We do not know her first name for certain. We do not know when she was born or when she died. Nearly everything known about her fits in one line of a tenth-century book, and yet she has not been forgotten.

Around 987, a Baghdad bookseller named Ibn al-Nadim compiled a great catalogue of the books and scholars of his time. In his list of the makers of astrolabes he mentions a woman: al-Ijliya, daughter of the astrolabe-maker al-Ijli, who had trained under a master of the craft and worked at the court of Sayf al-Dawla, ruler of Aleppo in Syria from about 944 to 967. That is all. The name Mariam, by which she is widely known today, does not appear in that text, and none of her instruments is known to survive.

But the line says a lot. An astrolabe was a precision tool: a brass disc engraved with a map of the sky, used to tell the time, find the direction of Mecca and measure the height of the stars. Making one required mathematics, astronomy and a skilled engraver's hand. She did not invent it, as is sometimes claimed; it is far older.

She was good enough to work for a prince. Today, an asteroid bears her name.
lesson: Honesty about what we do not know is part of respecting the past. And remember that good work matters even when history keeps only one line about the person who did it.

title: Salah ad-Din Enters Jerusalem Without a Massacre
teaser: In 1187 the people of Jerusalem expected the same bloodshed their city had seen in 1099. What happened instead was remembered for centuries, even by his enemies.
story:
October 1187. Inside the walls of Jerusalem, people are terrified. They remember what happened when the Crusaders took the city in 1099: its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants were massacred. Now the army of Salah ad-Din — Saladin — surrounds them, and they expect the same.

Saladin, sultan of Egypt and Syria, had defeated the Crusader army at Hattin three months earlier. After a short siege, the city's defender, Balian of Ibelin, came out to negotiate. The agreement reached was that the city would surrender without bloodshed, and that its inhabitants could buy their freedom for a fixed ransom and leave in safety.

On 2 October, Saladin's troops entered Jerusalem. There was no massacre. Guards protected the departing columns on the road. The arrangement was not gentle for everyone: many who could not pay were taken into captivity, as was the custom of the age. But chroniclers on both sides record that Saladin and his brother freed large numbers of the poor without payment, the elderly among them.

The Church of the Holy Sepulchre was left standing, and Eastern Christians remained in the city. Even in Europe, Saladin was long remembered as a chivalrous enemy who kept his word.
lesson: Strength shows its true quality at the moment of victory. When you have the upper hand, keep your word and choose mercy over revenge.

title: The Taj Mahal: Grief Turned Into Marble
teaser: An emperor lost his wife in 1631. The tomb he built for her on a riverbank at Agra is so carefully designed that even its letters are sized to look equal from the ground.
story:
In 1631, in the middle of a military campaign, the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan lost his wife. Mumtaz Mahal died giving birth to their fourteenth child. The court chroniclers describe an emperor overcome by grief.

The following year, on the bank of the river Yamuna at Agra, in northern India, work began on her tomb. Thousands of craftsmen and labourers took part. White marble was brought from Makrana, in Rajasthan, hundreds of kilometres away. The main building rose in about a decade, and the whole complex, with its mosque, gateway and gardens, was complete by about 1653.

Everything in it is balance. The tomb stands at the end of a long garden divided by water channels, an image of the gardens of Paradise. Verses of the Qur'an frame the great arches, designed by the calligrapher Amanat Khan; the letters grow larger as they climb, so that from the ground they all seem the same size. Flowers of coloured stone are set into the marble.

Shah Jahan died in 1666 and was buried beside his wife. The popular tale that the workers' hands were cut off so that they could never build its equal has no historical basis.
lesson: Sorrow can be turned into something that gives beauty to others. And before repeating a dramatic story, ask whether it is actually true.

title: Ibn Khaldun and the Science of Societies
teaser: Worn out by court intrigues, a statesman withdrew to a remote fortress to answer one question: why do kingdoms rise, and why do they fall?
story:
In 1375, a tired statesman shut himself away in a small fortress in the countryside of what is now Algeria. He had served several courts, and had known both favour and prison. Now he wanted to understand: why do kingdoms rise, and why do they fall?

Ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis in 1332, into a family of Andalusian origin. As a teenager he lost his parents and several of his teachers to the Black Death. For some twenty years he lived the dangerous life of a court official, from Fez to Granada.

In the fortress of Ibn Salama he began a history of the world, and completed the first draft of its introduction, the Muqaddima, in 1377. In it he asks historians to stop repeating tales and to check whether what they report is even possible. He studies how climate, work, trade, taxes and education shape societies. And he describes a force he calls asabiyya, the solidarity that binds a group together: strong among those who live a hard life, it lets them build a state, then fades with comfort, generation after generation.

He ended his life as a judge and teacher in Cairo, where he died in 1406. Many see in him a forerunner of sociology and economics.
lesson: Step back from events to look for their causes. Whoever understands why things happen, instead of only what happened, is better prepared for what comes next.
